---
title: "Joint probability of events"
---

Suppose that we want to know how often a pronoun is both plural and accusative. This question concerns the intersection of the plural and accusative events.

Return to the four form sample space

$$
\Omega_4=\{\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}
$$

with the probability measure below.

| outcome | probability |
|---|---:|
| *he* | $.20$ |
| *him* | $.30$ |
| *they* | $.10$ |
| *them* | $.40$ |

Let $P$ be the plural event and $A$ the accusative event:

$$
P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}
$$

and

$$
A=\{\textit{him},\textit{them}\}.
$$

The [**joint probability**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) of $P$ and $A$ is the probability assigned to their intersection:

$$
\mathbb{P}(P\cap A).
$$

We will sometimes abbreviate this quantity as $\mathbb{P}(P,A)$. The comma is shorthand for the intersection. It does not introduce another probability operation.

## The joint probability

Begin with the set operation:

$$
P\cap A=\{\textit{them}\}.
$$

Then apply the probability measure:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)
&=\mathbb{P}(\{\textit{them}\})\\
&=.40.
\end{aligned}
$$

The event containing outcomes that are both plural and accusative receives $.40$ of the total probability. This does not mean that $.40$ of plural forms are accusative. That question restricts attention to the plural event and requires conditional probability.

## Arrange all joint events in a table

The number distinction $P$ versus $P^c$ and the case distinction $A$ versus $A^c$ divide the sample space into four nonoverlapping intersections.

| | accusative $A$ | nominative $A^c$ | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| plural $P$ | *them*: $.40$ | *they*: $.10$ | $.50$ |
| singular $P^c$ | *him*: $.30$ | *he*: $.20$ | $.50$ |
| total | $.70$ | $.30$ | $1$ |

The upper right cell represents

$$
P\cap A^c=\{\textit{they}\},
$$

so its probability is $.10$. The lower left cell represents

$$
P^c\cap A=\{\textit{him}\},
$$

so its probability is $.30$.

The four interior cells are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Their probabilities must sum to one:

$$
.40+.10+.30+.20=1.
$$

The row and column totals are [**marginal probabilities**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html). For instance,

$$
\mathbb{P}(P)=.40+.10=.50.
$$

To obtain this marginal probability, we sum across both case values. The result is the probability of the plural event without any restriction on case.

## Reconstruct the table in base R

The following code stores the four joint probabilities in a matrix and computes its margins.

```{r}
#| eval: false
joint <- matrix(
  c(.40, .30, .10, .20),
  nrow = 2,
  dimnames = list(
    number = c("plural", "singular"),
    case = c("accusative", "nominative")
  )
)

joint
rowSums(joint)
colSums(joint)
sum(joint)
```

The row sums are $.50$ and $.50$, the column sums are $.70$ and $.30$, and the four cells sum to one. These are the margins and total shown in the table.

## Information in the joint distribution

A joint distribution records how probability is divided across both distinctions at once. Two corpora can both have $\mathbb{P}(P)=.50$ and $\mathbb{P}(A)=.70$ while assigning different probabilities to $P\cap A$. The marginal probabilities alone do not tell us which joint distribution we have.

If plural forms are more often accusative than singular forms, the four cells must reflect that association. The margins cannot show it by themselves.

## Marginal and joint probabilities

A marginal probability cannot replace an intersection probability. In the toy model, $\mathbb{P}(A)=.70$ includes both *him* and *them*. It cannot answer the question about forms that are both plural and accusative because it also includes singular accusative mass.

To compute the joint probability, translate *and* into an intersection, identify the outcomes in that intersection, and then apply $\mathbb{P}$.

## Check your understanding

1. Write the event represented by each of the four interior cells in the table.
2. Compute $\mathbb{P}(P^c\cap A^c)$ by listing the outcomes first.
3. Explain why $\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)=.40$ does not mean that $40\%$ of plural forms are accusative.
4. Construct a different four cell table with the same row and column margins but with $\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)=.35$.

Joint probability measures an intersection relative to the full sample space. The [next page](conditional-probability.qmd) restricts the comparison to one event and rescales the probability within it.
